Owen
J.A.:—In agreement with my colleague, Mr. Justice Monet, I
would maintain the present appeal, with costs, and dispose of the appeal in the
manner he suggests.

[

]

Under the former law (the
Code of
Civil Procedure
, 1965 Que. c. 80
(C.C.P.)
, arts. 332-381, repealed
1976, c. 9, s. 56 — now R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-25) Mr. Snyder proceeded by way of
jury trial against The Gazette in an action claiming a total of $735,360 for
actual and moral damages resulting from the publication of libellous statements
contained in an article which appeared in the newspaper on March 13, 1975.

[
3
]

In plaintiff's amended declaration, the
claim was set out as follows (pp. 18-9, J.C.):

45. Plaintiff estimates at the
present time that, as a result of said libellous statements, he has suffered in
addition to, and distinct from, any additional damages Plaintiff is entitled to
claim from third parties, the following damages from Defendant;

(a) Actual damages for injurious effect on his present and
future public career and on his future earnings

$367,680.00

(b) Pain, suffering, anguish and
humiliation

$122,560.00

(c) Moral damages

$245,120.00

[
4
]

The last four questions which the jury
was called upon to answer, together with the answers, were as follows (pp.
914-5, J.C.):

26 — Was Plaintiff Gerald Snyder
defamed by the article published in the Montreal Gazette?

Yes (6 — 0)

27 — If you have answered question
#26 in the affirmative, did Plaintiff Gerald Snyder suffer any damages as a
direct and immediate result of the publication of the article of the Montreal
Gazette and independently of any damages that he may also have suffered as a
result of the publication of similar statements in other news media?

Yes (6 — 0)

28 — If you have answered question #
27 in the affirmative, at what amount do you assess:

(a) the actual and real damages
suffered by Plaintiff Gerald Snyder for injurious effect on his public career,
up to the date of service of his action on the Montreal Gazette on May 27,
1975?

None (6 — 0)

(b) the actual and real damages
suffered by Plaintiff for injurious effect on his public career and on his
earnings since May 27, 1975 and in the future?

None (6 — 0)

(c) the moral damages suffered by
Plaintiff, including pain, suffering, anguish and humiliation?

$135,000.00 (6 — 0)

29 — If you have answered questions
# 26 and 27 in the affirmative, should the judgment of this Court be published
in the Montreal Gazette, at its expense, in as conspicuous a place as the
article complained of?

Yes (6 — 0)

[
5
]

Thus the jury, by their answers to the questions
put to them, held

(a) that Mr. Snyder was defamed by
the article published in The Gazette;

(b) that he did not thereby suffer
any actual and real damages either past or future; and

(c) that as a direct and immediate
result of the publication of the article in The Gazette and independently of
any damages that he may also have suffered as a result of the publication of
similar statements in other news media, Mr. Snyder suffered moral damages
including pain, suffering, anguish, and humiliation assessed at $135,000.

[
6
]

At the time art. 380 provided:

380. The judge shall render judgment
in conformity with the verdict unless it appears to him to be unreasonable.

[
7
]

The plaintiff moved for a judgment in
conformity with the verdict and the defendant moved for a judgment reducing the
award (p. 915, J.C.).

[
8
]

The presiding judge, after dealing with
the verdict as a whole (pp. 916-9, J.C.) considered the amount of the jurors'
award and stated that the $135,000 for moral damages was the only contentious
issue (p. 920, J.C.).

[
9
]

The court pointed out that seven other
actions were pending for amounts totalling $4,325,710 and that the present
action for $735,260 was the first to proceed.

[
10
]

The court stated that if The Gazette
were found at fault it should only be condemned to pay such damages as it has
itself caused, irrespective of any damages possibly flowing from the conduct of
other news media (p. 924, J.C.). The court also stated that the jury was
clearly instructed that our law does not allow granting of punitive damages (p.
927, J.C.). The court then asked itself the question: "Is the award
unreasonable?" (p. 929, J.C.). It pointed out that there are still pending
seven other actions by plaintiffs against various persons as a result of
similar libels and that the jury was well aware of that situation and must be
taken to have given it the necessary consideration (p. 935, J.C.). Finally, the
court came to the conclusion that the amount of the verdict ($135,000 for moral
or non-pecuniary damages) was not unreasonable and that it should be confirmed
(p. 937, J.C.) [
see
1978 CanLII 2184 (QC CS)
,
87 D.L.R. (3d) 5
,
[1978] Que S.C. 628
].

[
11
]

On the present appeal from the judgment
confirming the verdict in a civil jury trial this court has wide powers which
are set out in art. 381
C.C.P.
:

381. The judgment is subject to
appeal in the same manner as any final judgment of the Superior Court. The
Court of Appeal may confirm or reverse the judgment or order a new trial,
applying the remedy by which it considers that the ends of justice will best be
attained, even if it has not been specifically demanded.

[
12
]

I am, with respect, of the opinion that
the presiding judge should not have rendered judgment in conformity with such
verdict.

[
13
]

In my opinion the jury's award of
$135,000 for non-pecuniary or moral damages including pain, suffering, anguish,
and humiliation as the share of one defendant, The Gazette, "independently
of any damages that he (Mr. Snyder) may also have suffered as a result of the
publication of similar statements in other news media" is clearly unreasonable.
I would reduce the assessment of $135,000 to $13,500.

[
14
]

Eight separate actions have been taken
on behalf of Mr. Snyder. One action is against two persons, Guay and Dufour,
alleged to be responsible for defamatory statements, based on hearsay, made at
a hearing before the Quebec Police Commission. Seven actions are against
newspapers and other news media which published these statements. These eight
actions and the amounts claimed from each of the defendants for actual or
pecuniary damages and for moral or non-pecuniary damages are as follows:

[
15
]

In the present case we are dealing
solely with non-pecuniary damages. Mr. Snyder has made excessive claims
totalling $2,680,535 for non-pecuniary damages arising out of defamation.

[
16
]

The amounts claimed for non-pecuniary
damages in various types of actions have been spiralling upwards. Here we have
an extreme example in a libel action where one man evaluates at $2,680,535 his
non-pecuniary damages, that is moral damages including pain, suffering,
anguish, and humiliation arising out of statements made at an inquiry and
reports thereof in various media. He takes eight distinct civil actions and
brings only the present action on for trial before a judge and jury.

[
17
]

The same problem of excessive claims
and awards for non-pecuniary damages arose in connection with actions for
personal injuries. By three judgments delivered on January 19, 1978, sometimes
referred to as the "trilogy", the Supreme Court of Canada put a check
on the escalating amounts being claimed and awarded in Canada for non-pecuniary
damages in personal injury actions.

1.
Andrews
et al.
v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.
et al.
(1978),
1978 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, 83 D.L.R. (3d) 452, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229, [1978] 1 W.W.R. 577

[
18
]

This was a negligence action for
personal injury involving a young man rendered a quadriplegic in a traffic
accident. For non-pecuniary loss the trial court awarded $150,000 which the Court
of Appeal confirmed, and the Supreme Court of Canada reduced to $100,000.

[
19
]

Mr. Justice Dickson in delivering the
judgment of the court wrote as follows (at pp. 475-6 D.L.R., pp. 260-1 S.C.R.):

2.
Non-Pecuniary Losses

Andrews used to be a healthy young man,
athletically active and socially congenial. Now he is a cripple, deprived of
many of life's pleasures and subjected to pain and disability. For this, he is
entitled to compensation. But the problem here is qualitatively different from
that of pecuniary losses. There is no medium of exchange for happiness. There
is no market for expectation of life. The monetary evaluation of non-pecuniary
losses is a philosophical and policy exercise more than a legal or logical one.
The award must be fair and reasonable, fairness being gauged by earlier
decisions; but the award must also of necessity be arbitrary or conventional.
No money can provide true restitution. Money can provide for proper care: this
is the reason that I think the paramount concern of the Courts when awarding
damages for personal injuries should be to assure that there will be adequate
future care.

However, if the principle of the
paramountcy of care is accepted, then it follows that there is more room for
the consideration of other policy factors in the assessment of damages for
non-pecuniary losses. In particular, this is the area where the social burden
of large awards deserves considerable weight. The sheer fact is that there is
no objective yardstick for translating non-pecuniary losses, such as pain and
suffering and loss of amenities, into monetary terms. This area is open to
widely extravagant claims. It is in this area that awards in the United States
have soared to dramatically high levels in recent years. Statistically, it is
the area where the danger of excessive burden of expense is greatest.

[
20
]

Still dealing with non-pecuniary losses
Mr. Justice Dickson further stated (at pp. 477-8 D.L.R., pp. 263-4 S.C.R.):

Cases like the present enable the
Court to establish a rough upper parameter on these awards. It is difficult to
conceive of a person of his age losing more than Andrews has lost. Of course,
the figures must be viewed flexibly in future cases in recognition of the
inevitable differences in injuries, the situation of the victim, and changing
economic conditions.

The amounts of such awards should
not vary greatly from one part of the country to another. Everyone in Canada,
wherever he may reside, is entitled to a more or less equal measure of
compensation for similar non-pecuniary loss. Variation should be made for what
a particular individual has lost in the way of amenities and enjoyment of life,
and for what will function to make up for this loss, but variation should not
be made merely for the Province in which he happens to live.

There has been a significant
increase in the size of awards under this head in recent years. As Moir, J.A.,
of the Appellate Division of the Alberta Supreme Court, has warned: "To my
mind, damages under the head of loss of amenities will go up and up until they
are stabilized by the Supreme Court of Canada":
Hamel et al. v. Prather
et al.

(1976),
1976 ALTASCAD 3 (CanLII)
,
66 D.L.R. (3d) 109
at p. 127,
[1976] 2 W.W.R. 742
at p. 748
.
In my opinion, this time has come.

[
21
]

Mr. Justice Dickson concluded (at p.
478 D.L.R., p. 265 S.C.R.):

I would adopt as the appropriate
award in the case of a young adult quadriplegic like Andrews the amount of
$100,000. Save in exceptional circumstances, this should be regarded as an
upper limit of non-pecuniary loss in cases of this nature.

2. Thornton et al. v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57
(Prince George) et al. (1978),
1978 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, 83 D.L.R. (3d) 480, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 267, [1978]
1 W.W.R. 607

[
22
]

Mr. Justice Dickson again delivered the
judgment of the court and began by stating that the issues raised in this
appeal are essentially those raised
in the
Andrews
case (at p. 481
D.L.R., p. 271 S.C.R.):

The accident occurred as a result of
the negligence of the school authorities of the City of Prince George in
failing to exercise due care during physical education classes. While the
appellant was attempting a somersault, he sustained a serious flexion injury to
his neck with comminuted fracture of the fourth cervical vertebrae. The injury
caused total or partial paralysis to each of his four limbs. Prior to the injury
the appellant was 6′3″ in height and described in evidence as being
the epitome of the all-round athlete. At the date of trial he was 18 years of
age, physically disabled, unemployable, and wholly dependent upon male orderly
assistance for his day-to-day needs, yet with mental faculties wholly intact.

[
23
]

In this case the trial judge assessed
the non-pecuniary damages at $200,000 which was confirmed by the Court of
Appeal but reduced to $100,000 by the Supreme Court of Canada.

[
24
]

In dealing with non-pecuniary losses
Mr. Justice Dickson concluded as follows (at p. 490 D.L.R., p. 284 S.C.R.):

It will be recalled that, under this
heading, the trial Judge assessed the sum of $200,000. The Court of Appeal was
of the opinion that the amount awarded by the trial Judge, though generous, was
not so inordinately high as to constitute a wholly erroneous award. The Court
considered that there was little to distinguish the condition of the appellant
in this case from that of the appellant
in the
Andrews
case. The Court
of Appeal made no reduction under this head in the sum of $200,000.

The award under non-economic related
heads of damage should be a Canadian conventional award, adjusted to meet the
specific circumstances of the individual case. I am in agreement with the Court
of Appeal that the pain and suffering, loss of amenities, loss of enjoyment of
life and loss of expectation of life experienced by Thornton are essentially
similar to that experienced by Andrews. Both were active young men with an
abundance of life's pleasures before them. Both are now quadriplegics, although
both are mentally unimpaired and both are mobile when provided with proper
assistance. For the reasons expressed by me in
Andrews
I would reduce
the award for non-pecuniary loss to $100,000.

3.
Arnold
et al.
v. Teno
et al.

(1978),
1978 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, 83 D.L.R. (3d) 609, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 287, 3 C.C.L.T. 272

[
25
]

In this case Mr. Justice Spence (with
whom the other members of the court agreed on the question of non-pecuniary
damages) pointed out [at p. 612 D.L.R., p. 295 S.C.R.] that
in the
Andrews

and
Thornton
cases "...
the plaintiffs were young men who became
quadriplegic as a result of their injuries, although their mental capacities
were unaffected, while in the present appeal the plaintiff's mobility was very
seriously lessened although technically she was not paralyzed and she suffered
a very considerable degree of mental impairment".

[
26
]

In this case as
in the
Thornton

case the trial judge, for non-pecuniary damages, awarded $200,000 which was
approved by the Court of Appeal and reduced to $100,000 by the Supreme Court of
Canada.

[
27
]

On the question of non-pecuniary
damages Mr. Justice Spence concluded as follows (at p. 640 D.L.R., pp. 334-5
S.C.R.):

I am in respectful agreement with
Dickson, J., that there should be uniformity, always allowing flexibility to
meet each differing individual case, in awards for non-pecuniary damages.
Perhaps one should say there must be upper limits with awards lower in some
cases and some higher in exceptional cases. Dickson, J., has found $100,000 as
being the upper limit in both
Andrews
and
Thornton.
As I have
pointed out, those were both cases of young men turned by the accidents into
quadriplegics but whose mental faculties were unimpaired and who, by use of
wheelchairs and appropriate automotive vehicles, will be able to get about
amongst their fellow men.

The infant plaintiff Diane Teno,
although not completely paralyzed, is so disabled that her very limited ability
to walk is accomplished in such an awkward fashion as to cause her continual
embarrassment. Her left arm is very clumsy, her right is useless because of
spastic weakness, her speech is impaired and nearly unintelligible and her
mental impairment has reduced her to the "dull normal range". I am of
the opinion that such a condition justifies a very generous award to permit the
infant plaintiff to find some way by which her life may be made a little more
tolerable. Moreover, the infant plaintiff in the present appeal has a life
expectancy of 66.9 years while Andrews has a life expectancy of only 45 years
and Thornton only 49 years. Therefore, despite the fact that the infant
plaintiff, unlike Andrews and Thornton, will not need the frequent actual
treatment required by the latter such as turning in bed every two hours, the
other circumstances to which I have referred justify the allowance of the same
sum of $100,000 to her under this heading of non-pecuniary damages.

[
28
]

If the upper limit for total
non-pecuniary damages in the case of a young person rendered a quadriplegic is
$100,000, what should the upper limit for total non-pecuniary damages in the
case of a middle-aged person who has been defamed? In my opinion the pain,
suffering, anguish, and humiliation of Mr. Snyder whose reputation has been
attacked, but vindicated by a judgment holding the attacks unjustified, is not
anywhere near equivalent to the pain, suffering, anguish, and humiliation of a
quadriplegic. In the light of the holdings of the Supreme Court of Canada in
the "trilogy" referred to above, Mr. Snyder's total non-pecuniary damages
should be less, considerably less, than $100,000.

[
29
]

In assessing The Gazette's share of Mr.
Snyder's total non-pecuniary damages at $135,000, the jury must have concluded
that the total amount of Mr. Snyder's non-pecuniary damages arising from the defamation
was many times greater than $135,000. In the action against The Gazette Mr.
Snyder claimed as non-pecuniary damages $367,680. In the seven other actions
Mr. Snyder claimed as non-pecuniary damages a total of $2,312,855. To arrive at
the figure of $135,000 as The Gazette's share of Mr. Snyder's non-pecuniary
damages the jury, if acting reasonably, must have calculated that Mr. Snyder's
total non-pecuniary damages were practically $1,000,000.

[
30
]

The jury's verdict in evaluating The
Gazette's share of Mr. Snyder's total non-pecuniary damages at $135,000 appears
patently unreasonable.

[
31
]

On the ground that the upper limit of
the total non-pecuniary damages that Mr. Snyder is reasonably entitled to
recover as a result of the eight different actions should be less than $100,000
and on the ground that the jury's award of $135,000 as The Gazette's share of
Mr. Snyder's total non-pecuniary damages must be predicated on total
non-pecuniary damages of almost $1,000,000, I have come to the conclusion that
the verdict of $135,000 against The Gazette is unreasonable.

[
32
]

The remaining problem is to fix a
reasonable amount representing The Gazette's share of Mr. Snyder's total
non-pecuniary damages. These moral damages cannot be calculated with anything
resembling mathematical precision.

[
33
]

In the case of
Arnold v. Teno
,
referred to above, Mr. Justice Spence stated (at pp. 638-9 D.L.R., p. 332
S.C.R.):

The real difficulty is that an award
of non-pecuniary damages cannot be "compensation". There is simply no
equation between paralyzed limbs and/or injured brain and dollars. The award is
not reparative: there can be no restoration of the lost function. There can be
no doubt that awards for non-pecuniary damages in the immediate past have been
increasing apace. In the case of many verdicts in the United States, it may
well be said that they have been soaring. The reasons probably are many.
Firstly, I have pointed out the impossibility of accurate assessment. Then
there must be many cases of what really are expressions of deep sympathy for
the terribly injured plaintiff and a mistaken feeling that his or her sore loss
of the amenities of life may be assuaged by the feeling of satisfaction from a
pocket-full of money. There might even be some element of punishment for the
wrongdoer or, the most irrelevant of considerations, a measuring of the depth
of the defendant's purse. Certainly, such awards, which one may well
characterize as exorbitant, fail to accord with the requirement of
reasonableness, a proper gauge for all damages.

This reasoning is applicable to an
award of non-pecuniary damages in a defamation case.

[
34
]

Various factors may be taken into
consideration as guides to assist in arriving at a reasonable global sum to be
awarded for such damages. Some of these factors have been discussed by my
colleague Mr. Justice Monet in arriving at his "well-reasoned guess"
of $13,500. I might mention one of the factors which I considered in reaching
the same figure. In the eight actions taken by Mr. Snyder the total amount
claimed for non-pecuniary damages is $2,680,535. For the reasons set out above,
I consider the upper limit for total non-pecuniary damages in the eight actions
to be less than $100,000. In other words in the eight actions Mr. Snyder is
claiming at least 27 times the upper limit. Dividing the total amount claimed
in the eight actions, $2,680,535, by 27 gives a quotient of $99,279. Dividing
the sum claimed in the action against The Gazette, $367,680, by 27 gives a
quotient of $13,618. This is another indication that the figure of $13,500 is a
reasonable amount.

[
35
]

For these reasons I would maintain the
appeal, with costs, and dispose thereof in the manner suggested by my colleague
Mr. Justice Monet.

[
36
]

[

]

The verdict is contained in the replies
given by the jury to several questions. For the purposes of the appeal, the
most important of these are as follows:

[
38
]

In his amended declaration (art. 45,
record 18) the respondent, claiming $735,360, said as follows:

present time that, as a result of said libellous statements, he has suffered

his future earnings

$367,680.00

damages

$245,120.00

As we see, the claims listed in arts.
45(b) and 45(c) were included in Q. 28(c).

[
39
]

In his memorandum dated April 23, 1979,
the appellant concluded as follows (p. 19):

For all the foregoing reasons,
Appellant respectfully prays that the Judgment be set aside on the ground that
the damages awarded were excessive; that the damages be reduced to the sum of
$13,500.00 or that, in the alternative, a new trial be ordered on the issue of
moral damages alone.

[
40
]

This case arose from the testimony of a
police officer which was reported in an issue of the appellant's newspaper.

[
41
]

The
testimony of the police officer
,
Constable Henri Dufour, was given on March 12, 1975, before the Police
Commission, dealing with a petition with respect to the dismissal of André
Guay, assistant director of police for the Montreal Urban Community. (A claim
for damages of $500,000 against Dufour and Guay jointly and severally was
instituted by the respondent in this case.) The transcript of Dufour's
testimony (ex. P-7), when questioned by Guay's lawyer, is as follows (record,
pp. 199-200, 201-2):

Then he (superior officer) asked me
if I had already encountered obstruction in my police work. I asked him what he
meant. He said: "the beat you were on today, I don't have to tell you that
you were close to the really big one, from the point of view ..." he left
me to understand ...

• • • • •

Q Then, what did Mr. (superior
officer) say to you. You were up against about the most powerful one, did he
tell you who was the most powerful, what was it, who was the most powerful?

A Do I have to tell you the name of
the person involved ...

Chairman:

Just a minute. Hold on for a minute,
we'll come back to that, we'll order that the session be held
in camera

presently.

A Right.

Just a moment. We're going to order
that the session be held
in camera
right away. Police officers and
journalists may stay in the room. Others must leave the room.

Lawyer for
Mr. Guay:

Q Who was this person who was the
most important or the most dangerous?

A Mr. Gerry Snyder. He, at that
point, when he told me his name, he told me that for him, without giving me any
other explanation, that Mr. Gerry Snyder was, in his opinion, the
representative of the Jewish Mafia here in Montreal.

[
42
]

The
publication
on March 13,
1975, of this part of the testimony in the appellant's newspaper (ex. P-1) is
headed:

FORMER CITY OFFICIAL CALLED MEMBER OF "JEWISH MAFIA"

The first paragraph of the publication
reads:

A former vice-chairman of the
executive committee of Montreal and now a member of the COJO board of directors
was described yesterday by police as the "representative of the Jewish
Mafia in Montreal".

This text appears beside a photograph
below which is written on the first line and in capital letters
"Henri Dufour",
and on the
second line in small letters: "... boss told him".

[
43
]

For the purposes of this opinion, I
believe that it is useful to reproduce the following exhibits as an appendix:

But the respect which a verdict

necessarily assumes a prior process which consists of weighing the various
elements likely to tip the balance one way or the other.

the jury evaluate the evidence in a manner different from that of a legal

(b) Publication

[

In my view, publication is usually an

of the

[

An order for costs is a legal
obligation, not depending upon fault, which flows from the idea that the party
which wins should be compensated for the costs of the trial by the party which
is defeated. In practice, this idea rarely coincides with concrete reality.
Costs in our system of law are
inter partes.

[
108

Fees, as I see them in our system, are
the fair fees, known as extrajudicial which a lawyer has a right to demand of
his client; moreover, they are often called "solicitor to client
fees". In fixing these fees, the lawyer takes into account, if necessary,
expenses paid by the other party (reg. 3.08.08 with respect to the Code of
Ethics). But this is something quite different from costs.

[
109

Previously, I explained my concerns
with respect to the expenses which inevitably arise from the trial at first

favour of the applicant is amended by the court, for example, by changing the

I believe that it would be wrong to deceive ourselves by overlooking this
practical aspect; it seems to me that judges would be wrong to underestimate

For my part, with the greatest respect,

Drapeau

I deem it important that a person

appeals, with costs.
You do not have to be a genius to know that the total
taxable costs of the six appellants amounted to or exceeded $2,000.

[

Today, twenty years after the
Drapeau

the comments of my colleague, Mr. Justice Monet, but with respect I do not

[

From the outset it is accepted, since
this part of the final judgment is not disputed here, that the respondent was

inter alia

newspaper's large circulation.

[

The jury, whose other findings are not
challenged, came to the unanimous conclusion that the amount of $135,000
represented the amount of damage suffered by the respondent. I do not deny that
the amount is considerable and exceeds by far the amounts usually granted in
such cases in Canada. Incidentally, I will not engage in a comparative study of

[
122
]

However, whether or not the amount is
large, the question is simply whether the amount of damages granted by the jury

[

Of course, as my colleague quite

[

Appellant also pretends shock at the
possibility that cumulative awards might give Respondent substantial

difference in the moral consequences of a libel confined to a limited circle or

millions of individuals. The undersigned cannot refer to a single precedent in
the Canadian history where the libel against an individual appears to have been
so extensive both in gravity and in distribution. If it turns out that
Respondent has been libelled viciously before half the population of Canada, the

because the compensation required to repair the harm done might appear to
represent considerable sums.

[
129

Did the jury, in spite of having been
correctly instructed on each of the points which the appellant cites as having

87 D.L.R. (3d) 5
,
[1978] Que. S.C. 628

... must depend to a large extent
upon the value which the community is prepared to put on the reputation of its
members, especially those in public life.

And he continued (record, pp. 933-4
[pp. 17-8 D.L.R., p. 635 Que. S.C.]):

In this field, juries are especially
apt at determining the propriety of a compensation. They represent the views of
a cross-section of society and should mirror the generally accepted opinion as
to the value of the reputation of an honest public man. Indeed in the United
Kingdom as well as in Canada, the assessment of those damages by juries has
been consistently higher than that by Judges, either at trial or in appeal.

Now that is the very function and
purpose of the institution of the jury and recent events in another field of
law have shown that juries, expressing public opinion, can powerfully alter the
course of justice and bring to the fore the necessity of adapting the law to

In this case, the jury was composed
of a lady clerk, an artist, a truck driver, a retired executive, a female sales
clerk and a shipping manager. They accepted the plaintiff's version of the

had brought damages over himself by his own act (Q. 12), they found that the

plaintiff had been entrusted with the delicate and important task of generating
the revenue necessary to finance the Olympic Games.

Even though plaintiff has not
suffered financially from the blow, the jury obviously thought that he must

judgment, would fairly compensate in our times a public man so unjustly and
widely libelled.

This Court is not prepared to say
that the jury's estimate is so grossly inflated as to be branded as
unreasonable, in the light of all the circumstances of the case.

In conclusion (record, p.
937 [p. 19 D.L.R., p. 636 Que. S.C.]):

One's reputation is probably one's
most valuable and cherished property: money does little good to a man of ill
fame in honest society. Too often do we hear about the misgivings of otherwise
able men concerning public life: they cherish their reputation and they fear to
put it in jeopardy, should they decide to devote their life to public affairs.

The jury that heard the present case
has given us a lesson. Time has passed when merely nominal damages were
considered sufficient retribution for defamation. If society wants, as it
should, that its best citizens turn to public affairs, it must show the high
esteem in which it holds them; and those who would imprudently risk, by a
stroke of the pen, to destroy the reputation of such dedicated men ought to be
prepared to pay the high price that such a misdeed deserves. The freedom of the
press can only be justified so long as the press itself shows its sense of
responsibility: it has failed in the present case.

The Court comes therefore to the
conclusion that the amount of the verdict is not unreasonable and should be
confirmed.

[
130
]

I agree with these views, and for the
same reasons, I am not ready to substitute my opinion for that of the jury and
the judge below.

[
131
]

For these reasons, with respect for the
contrary opinion, I would dismiss the appeal with costs.

]
